newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition plans ear-splitting gridlock.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition plans ear-splitting gridlock.

text.p: Serbian opposition leaders promise deafening, round-the-clock traffic jams in central Belgrade on Saturday, the 55th straight day of peaceful protests against poll fraud.
"Take you cars, take your whistles and trumpets, use you car horns, make a din to be remembered and do it non-stop on Saturday," Zajedno (Together) coalition leader Vuk Draskovic told his followers
Ear-splitting gridlock is the latest in a series of imaginative ploys by Zajedno, protesting against annulment of their victories in local elections on November 17 in Belgrade and 13 other cities.
"Take your cameras and take pictures together with the police. Record the historical moments for posterity," Draskovic told Belgraders who have been squaring off daily with hundreds of riot police.
But President Slobodan Milosevic won unexpected political support on Friday when former enemy Croatia said the Serbian opposition movement could be a threat to peace if it gained power.

"Croatia has no interest in favouring Milosevic...but at this moment the Serbian opposition does not offer any guarantees for maintaining the peace," said Zlatko Canjuga, a political adviser to nationalist President Franjo Tudjman.
Yugoslavia and Croatia, having fought a six-month war in 1991, established diplomatic relations late last year after a surprise Milosevic-Tudjman summit.
In an interview, Canjuga warned the international community about what he called dangerous nationalist rhetoric by leading figures in the Serbian opposition.
Both Tudjman and Milosevic have bad human rights records and encouraged mutual fear and hatred among their people.

Milosevic, facing the biggest challenge to his 10-year rule, has been abandoned by part of the army, the Orthodox Church and on Friday even by his normally staunch allies at the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. Even his Socialist Party is reported to be split between moderates and hardliners over whether to cack down on the protests.
Senior officials from the Socialist Party met on Friday with leaders of the Yugoslav United Left, which is headed by Milosevic's hardliner wife Mirjana Markovic.
A statement issued through state agency Tanjug declared that both parties wanted irregularities in local elections investigated "whichever side is damaged".

But it also slammed the daily demonstrations "as expansion of political conflicts with elements of violence and terrorism". It said they were instigated from abroad, disruptive for the country's development and damaging its standing abroad.
The government, it said, should "ensure efficient and responsible work of all state organs in keeping with the Constitution and laws of the country".
Milosevic has conceded his party's election loss in Serbia's second largest city Nis but failed to appease Zajedno leaders who vowed to continue protests until all their claims were met.
The United States said that admission of Zajedno's victory in Nis did not go far enough and Milosevic could not win world applause by "dribbling out minor concessions".
The major powers' Contact Group on former Yugoslavia meets in Brussels on Saturday and may add to the pressure on Milosevic.
"I have the impression that they are going to try to get a unified position," said a NATO source. "They will probably come out with a fairly strong statement."
The European Union has called on Milosevic to accept opposition victories and embrace democracy and human rights.
